# Data Curation and the Training Distribution {#sec-data-curation}

@sec-scaling-laws turns a compute budget into a model size and a number of
training tokens. It does not say which tokens to use. That choice is the job of
data curation.

At fixed architecture, optimizer, and token budget, selection and sampling are
major determinants of the model that training produces. They decide which
languages, domains, styles, and repeated patterns the model sees. They also
decide whether later evaluations measure generalization or accidental exposure
to benchmark answers. These effects must be measured for the target model and
evaluation suite; no universal quality score can choose the corpus in advance.

The output of curation is therefore a versioned training distribution:
source-specific shards, a sampling policy, exclusion decisions, lineage records,
and an **@gls-decontamination report** that states which benchmark-overlap
checks were run and what they removed.

## The run consumes a distribution, not a folder

Four quantities are easy to confuse:

1. The **acquisition pool** is everything collected from source snapshots.
2. The **retained corpus** is what remains after policy, extraction,
   deduplication, and quality decisions.
3. The **mixture** assigns sampling probabilities to retained sources.
4. The **training stream** is the ordered sequence of token instances consumed
   by the run.

A source can occupy 20 percent of stored bytes but receive 5 percent of sampled
tokens. A small source can be sampled for several effective epochs, meaning
several full passes over its data, while a large source is only partly read.
Corpus inventory is therefore not the same as the distribution learned by the
model.

The useful unit also changes by stage. Acquisition works with files, pages, and
repository revisions. Deduplication may work with documents, paragraphs, or
spans. The model consumes tokens. Every report should name its unit instead of
moving silently between documents, bytes, and tokens.

## Build lineage into every stage

The pipeline narrows the acquisition pool, but each rejection also creates
evidence. Counts, reason codes, policy versions, and stable record identifiers
must travel with the data.

```{figure}
//| figure: curation-retention
//| label: fig-data-curation-pipeline
//| fig-cap: "Per-stage retention in three published web-curation pipelines. The blue trunk is what survives; each branch is what one stage removed, colored by the kind of decision and labeled with the share of that stage's input it removed. DCLM-Baseline reports every share as a fraction of the original DCLM-Pool documents [@li2024dclm]. RefinedWeb reports document rates for URL filtering, text extraction, and language identification and token rates after them, so its later kept shares multiply the two units [@penedo2023refinedweb]. FineWeb counts tokens from the 36T left after base filtering, whose input it does not report [@penedo2024fineweb]. All numbers are as published."
```

These requirements can be stated as an algorithm:

```text
1. Freeze every acquired source as an immutable snapshot.
2. Attach provenance and a policy decision before content filtering.
3. Preserve stable record IDs through extraction and normalization.
4. Apply versioned policy, deduplication, and quality transforms.
5. Compare every retained stage, including synthetic data, with the
   frozen evaluation registry.
6. Write per-source shards, membership manifests, rejection statistics,
   and the sampling schedule.
7. Tokenize and pack with a pinned tokenizer and deterministic ordering.
```

This work usually runs on CPU-heavy batch infrastructure before the accelerator
training job begins. The pipeline needs resumability as well as throughput: a
failed stage should restart from immutable inputs without changing which records
survive.

## Decide whether a source may enter

Publicly reachable, crawlable, licensed, and consented are different
properties. Common Crawl supplies timestamped web captures; it does not grant a
single license over every captured page. Books, papers, code repositories,
licensed collections, and model-generated records need the same source-level
review.

A provenance record should include the source URL or repository revision,
retrieval time, raw-content digest, creator or publisher when known, stated
license and its evidence URL, and dated observations of relevant site terms or
crawl preferences. It should also record the project's documented basis for
use. Unknown or incompatible cases go to quarantine rather than quietly
entering the corpus. Longpre et al. found widespread missing and incorrectly
categorized licenses in their audit of more than 1,800 text datasets, which is
why a dataset-level label is not enough [@longpre2023provenance]. Legal
permissibility remains policy- and jurisdiction-dependent; @sec-data-rights-economics
covers those legal questions.

Personal-information control is also a multi-step process, in which pattern
matching such as a regular expression is one step. Define which classes are
excluded, combine rules and model-based detectors, review locale-specific
samples, and record detector versions and error rates. No detector proves that a
corpus contains no personal information. Flagged content needs restricted
access, and a complaint or removal request must be traceable forward to every
derived shard and training run. Audits of public corpora have found personal
information alongside duplicates, synthetic text, and benchmark material
[@elazar2024wimbd].

## Extract and normalize without erasing the source

Web captures contain markup, menus, cookie notices, broken character encodings,
and boilerplate copied across many pages. Extraction identifies the main text
and document boundaries. Normalization then applies a documented Unicode form,
repairs chosen extraction artifacts, and standardizes only the features the
pipeline has explicitly decided are irrelevant.

The raw and normalized content digests should both remain in lineage. A change
in Unicode handling, boilerplate removal, or whitespace rules changes exact
identity and can change later deduplication. Rebuilding with a new extractor
therefore produces a new corpus version and should be recorded as one.

Language identification is similarly fallible. A low confidence score may mean
mixed-language text, code switching (alternating languages within a passage),
transliteration, or a language the classifier represents poorly. Kreutzer et
al. found severe labeling and content quality problems in the multilingual web
corpora they audited, especially for lower-resource languages, those with little
available digital text [@kreutzer2022quality]. Report retention by language
and review affected samples with relevant language knowledge.

Filtering can also erase legitimate language varieties while appearing to
remove only undesirable text. Dodge et al. showed that C4's blocklist
disproportionately removed text from and about minority groups
[@dodge2021documenting]. Rules are easier to inspect than learned scorers,
which are trained models that rate text, but neither is inherently unbiased.

## Deduplicate at the unit that matters

Deduplication serves several different purposes:

- **Exact document deduplication** hashes canonicalized document bytes and
  removes identical records.
- **Exact span deduplication** uses a suffix array or another repeated-substring
  index to find long copied passages inside otherwise different documents.
- **Fuzzy document deduplication** compares sets of shingles, such as
  overlapping word sequences, to find documents with small edits.
- **Semantic deduplication** uses embeddings, vectors that place texts with
  similar meaning near one another, to find meaning-level similarity.
  It can catch rewrites that lexical methods miss, but it also imports the
  embedding model's definition of similarity [@abbas2023semdedup].

Removing redundancy can reduce memorization and save training steps. Lee et al.
found a tenfold reduction in verbatim memorization in their experiments, as well
as the same or better accuracy with fewer steps [@lee2022deduplicating]. The
result does not imply that more deduplication is always better. A global policy
can remove useful recurring material or leave an unusual remainder. FineWeb,
for example, selected per-crawl rather than global fuzzy deduplication after
controlled ablations, training comparisons that change one pipeline choice at a
time [@penedo2024fineweb].

### Jaccard similarity and MinHash

Represent a document $d$ as a set of shingles $S(d)$. The Jaccard similarity of
documents $a$ and $b$ is

$$
J(a,b)=\frac{|S(a)\cap S(b)|}{|S(a)\cup S(b)|}.
$$

Here $S(a)$ and $S(b)$ are the distinct shingle sets, $\cap$ is set
intersection, $\cup$ is set union, and $|\cdot|$ counts set elements. The value
is zero for disjoint sets and one for identical sets.

The formula requires $n(n-1)/2$ comparisons when applied to every pair of $n$
documents. @gls-minhash, introduced for document resemblance by Broder in 1997,
replaces each shingle set with a short randomized signature
[@broder1997resemblance]. For random permutation $\pi_i$ of the shingle
universe, define

$$
h_i(S)=\min_{x\in S}\pi_i(x),
\qquad
\widehat J(a,b)=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}
\mathbf{1}\!\left[h_i(S(a))=h_i(S(b))\right].
$$

The terms have the following meanings: $h_i(S)$ is the minimum permuted rank in
set $S$ under permutation $i$; $x$ is a shingle; $m$ is the signature length;
$\mathbf{1}[\cdot]$ is one when its
condition is true and zero otherwise; and $\widehat J$ is the estimated Jaccard
similarity. For ideal independent permutations,
$\mathbb{E}[\widehat J]=J$ and
$\operatorname{Var}(\widehat J)=J(1-J)/m$. More signature entries reduce
variance, although one realized estimate need not improve monotonically.

The @gls-lsh technique avoids the all-pairs comparison by hashing similar signatures
into shared buckets, so only documents that share a bucket are compared. It
splits each signature into $b$ bands of $r$ rows, so $m=br$. If two
documents have Jaccard similarity $s$, the idealized probability that at least
one band matches is

$$
P_{\mathrm{candidate}}(s)=1-\left(1-s^r\right)^b.
$$

The symbols mean the following: $P_{\mathrm{candidate}}(s)$ is the probability
of becoming a candidate pair; $s\in[0,1]$ is true Jaccard similarity; $b$ is the
number of bands; and $r$ is
the rows per band. More bands at fixed signature length increase candidate
recall and false positives. More rows per band make the gate stricter and can
increase false negatives. LSH produces candidates, not proof of duplication;
an implementation may verify candidates with exact Jaccard or another pinned
rule before forming duplicate clusters.

```{figure}
//| figure: lsh-banding
//| label: fig-data-curation-lsh-probability
//| fig-cap: "LSH banding on 300 illustrative document pairs. The curve is $P_{\mathrm{candidate}}(s)=1-(1-s^r)^b$ for the chosen $b$ bands of $r$ rows. Each dot is one pair at its true Jaccard similarity $s$, drawn uniformly from a fixed seed; its signature rows agree independently with probability $s$, the idealization behind the equation, and the pair sits in the upper strip when at least one band matched. Pairs with $s\geq\tau$ count as duplicates, so filled orange dots are false positives and hollow blue dots are false negatives; the shading marks the probability of each error at each similarity. The presets are the FineWeb setting and the two settings of Lee et al., which RefinedWeb reuses [@penedo2024fineweb; @lee2022deduplicating; @penedo2023refinedweb]. The grid shows the bands of the selected pair."
```

The cell below runs MinHash on two near-duplicate paragraphs, the second an
edited copy of the first. It shingles each into word 3-grams, replaces each
permutation $\pi_i$ with the hash $(c_1x+c_0)\bmod p$ that common
implementations use in its place, and draws 200 signatures at each length $m$.
It checks the two equations above: the estimates center on the exact $J$, and
their spread follows $\sqrt{J(1-J)/m}$ within 25% at every $m$, so the hashed
stand-in behaves like ideal permutations here. The histogram compares the
estimates at $m=32$ with the binomial distribution that the equations imply.
Set `w = 5` and $J$ drops from 0.70 to 0.56 for the same three edits, because
each changed word now breaks five shingles instead of three: the shingle width,
not the estimator, decides what counts as similar.

:::: {.runnable}
```python
import zlib
from math import comb
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

a = ("web text is crawled from billions of pages and many of them repeat each "
     "other with small changes such as a new date a different footer or a copied "
     "paragraph from a news wire so a curation pipeline removes near duplicates "
     "before training because repeated text is memorized more easily and wastes "
     "the compute budget on examples the model has already seen many times")
b = a.replace("new date", "fresh timestamp").replace("news wire", "press release")
b = b.replace("is memorized", "gets memorized")

w = 3  # shingle width in words; try 5
def shingles(text):
    t = text.split()
    return {zlib.crc32(" ".join(t[i:i + w]).encode()) for i in range(len(t) - w + 1)}
S_a, S_b = shingles(a), shingles(b)
J = len(S_a & S_b) / len(S_a | S_b)
U = np.array(sorted(S_a | S_b))
in_a, in_b = np.isin(U, list(S_a)), np.isin(U, list(S_b))

# h_i(S) = min over S of (c1 * x + c0) mod p: a hashed stand-in for a permutation.
p, pool = 2**31 - 1, 200 * 128
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
c1, c0 = rng.integers(1, p, pool), rng.integers(0, p, pool)
h = (c1[:, None] * (U % p)[None, :] + c0[:, None]) % p          # pool x |union|
match = h[:, in_a].min(1) == h[:, in_b].min(1)

ms = [4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128]
est = {m: match[:200 * m].reshape(200, m).mean(1) for m in ms}  # 200 signatures each
sd = [est[m].std() for m in ms]
ideal = [np.sqrt(J * (1 - J) / m) for m in ms]
for m, s, i in zip(ms, sd, ideal):  # Var = J(1 - J)/m holds for the hashed version
    assert abs(est[m].mean() - J) < 4 * i / np.sqrt(200) and 0.75 < s / i < 1.25

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.2, 6.2))
ax1.plot(ms, ideal, "--", c="C1", label="√(J(1−J)/m)")
ax1.plot(ms, sd, "o", c="C0", label="spread of 200 signatures")
ax1.set(xscale="log", yscale="log", xlabel="signature length m", ylabel="standard deviation of Ĵ")
ax1.set_xticks(ms, [str(m) for m in ms])
ax1.set_yticks([0.04, 0.06, 0.1, 0.2], ["0.04", "0.06", "0.1", "0.2"])
ax1.legend()
m = 32
k = np.arange(m + 1)
pmf = [comb(m, j) * J**j * (1 - J) ** (m - j) for j in k]
ax2.hist(est[m], bins=np.arange(m + 2) / m - 0.5 / m, color="C0", label=f"Ĵ, m = {m}")
ax2.plot(k / m, 200 * np.array(pmf), "o-", c="C1", ms=3, lw=1, label="Binomial(m, J) / m")
ax2.axvline(J, ls=":", c="grey")
ax2.set(xlabel="estimated Jaccard similarity", ylabel="signatures", xlim=(J - 0.4, J + 0.4))
ax2.legend(fontsize=9)
fig.suptitle(f"J = {J:.3f}: hashed MinHash is unbiased, variance J(1−J)/m")
fig.tight_layout()
print(f"{len(S_a)} and {len(S_b)} shingles, true J = {J:.3f}")
```
::::

@fig-data-curation-1 separates the all-pairs baseline from one favorable indexed
case and from the same index with one degenerate bucket. The terms in its bound are signature construction, which costs $O(nm)$,
and the $K$ candidate pairs emitted by the index, giving roughly $O(nm+K)$ work.
It is close to linear only when candidates per document stay bounded. In a degenerate
bucket, $K$ can still approach $n(n-1)/2$.

![Schematic comparison of fuzzy-dedup work on log axes. All-pairs comparison grows as n(n − 1)/2. The solid line is an index that emits eight candidate pairs per document, a favorable operating regime rather than an LSH worst-case guarantee. The dotted line is the same index with one degenerate bucket that holds 1% of the documents: its internal pairs, (0.01n)(0.01n − 1)/2, outnumber the other candidates once n passes about 160,000, and the work grows quadratically again.](/figures/data-curation-1.svg){#fig-data-curation-1}

Duplicate clusters must also be resolved deterministically. Sort records by a
stable identity, build all verified similarity edges, compute connected
components, and choose one representative by a pinned policy. Dropping a
document merely because it collided in an LSH bucket can delete distinct text;
choosing the first record seen makes the corpus depend on partition order.

## Quality is a measured property

There is no context-free label called “high-quality text.” A filter can favor
fluent prose while harming code, favor Wikipedia-like language while removing
conversation, or improve one evaluation while narrowing another domain.

Two broad tool families are common:

- **Rules** measure length, repetition, symbol ratios, boilerplate patterns,
  language confidence, or other inspectable features.
- **Learned scorers** estimate similarity to a reference set or predict a label
  such as educational value.

Neither family is inherently high-recall, high-precision, or unbiased until the
target is defined and checked against reviewed data. CCNet, for example, scores
documents by their perplexity under a reference language model, a measure of how
predictable that model finds the text. The score therefore measures similarity
to CCNet's Wikipedia-derived reference distribution, not an objective property
called fluency [@wenzek2020ccnet]. Report retention and error rates by relevant
language, dialect, geography, source, and topic slices. Inspect excluded records
as well as accepted ones.

The strongest validation is a fixed-budget training ablation. Hold the raw
pool, tokenizer, model, optimizer, token budget, and evaluation suite constant;
change one curation decision; then compare loss and downstream slices. FineWeb
publicly ablated extraction, filtering, and deduplication choices. DataComp-LM
later provided a 240-trillion-token raw pool and standardized model training to
compare data recipes, finding model-based filtering important in its baseline
setting [@penedo2024fineweb; @li2024dclm]. These are controlled results, not
universal rankings of datasets.

@fig-data-curation-2 shows the intended mechanism as a thought experiment. A
curated stream helps only if it yields more useful signal for the target
distribution per token consumed. Filtering that removes useful coverage can
move the curve the other way.

![Conceptual useful-token tradeoff. Under the illustrated assumption, a curated stream provides more relevant, non-redundant signal per sampled token than an unfiltered stream. The curves are not measured loss and are not a universal ordering of corpora.](/figures/data-curation-2.svg){#fig-data-curation-2}

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested

Scale and quality are not opposing camps. FineWeb is both large and heavily
filtered; FineWeb-Edu is a learned-filtered subset of crawled text, not a fully
generated corpus. RefinedWeb showed that filtered web-only data could outperform
several public mixed corpora in its experiments, while Dolma prioritized
documented source diversity [@penedo2023refinedweb; @soldaini2024dolma].
The open question is which acquisition pool, retention policy, mixture, and
schedule work for a stated model, budget, and evaluation target.
:::

## Turn retained sources into sampled tokens

Suppose the retained corpus has $K$ sources. Each static mixture defines

$$
P_{\mathrm{train}}(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_kP_k(x),
\qquad
w_k\geq 0,
\qquad
\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_k=1.
$$

The symbols mean the following: $P_{\mathrm{train}}(x)$ is the probability of
sampling token sequence $x$ for training; $P_k(x)$ is the sampling distribution
within source $k$; $w_k$ is
that source's mixture weight; and $K$ is the number of sources. With a total
budget of $D$ sampled tokens, source $k$ contributes an expected
$D_k=w_kD$ tokens.

If source $k$ contains $U_k$ retained token instances, the following formula
defines its expected effective epochs:

$$
e_k=\frac{D_k}{U_k}=\frac{w_kD}{U_k}.
$$

The terms mean the following: $e_k$ is the expected number of full passes over
source $k$; $D_k$ is its sampled-token allocation; and $U_k$ is its unique
retained-token count. This
quantity exposes accidental oversampling that a table of mixture percentages
can hide.

Weights can come from expert judgment or compute-matched proxy experiments.
DoReMi first trains a small reference model on initial domain weights, then
trains a same-size proxy with group distributionally robust optimization, which
shifts weight toward the domains where the proxy's loss most exceeds the
reference model's (the per-domain excess loss). It averages the evolving weights
and uses them to resample data for a larger model [@xie2023doremi]. The reported
transfer from a 280M proxy to an 8B model is evidence from that experiment; it
is not guaranteed to hold across tokenizers, domain definitions, model families,
or scales.

A static mixture holds each $w_k$ fixed. A curriculum uses time-dependent weights
$w_k(t)$ or changes example ordering as training progresses. Late up-weighting
of a high-quality or domain-specific slice is one form of curriculum, often
called data annealing or a cool-down mixture when paired with the final
learning-rate phase. Its interaction with the training schedule is
covered in @sec-mid-training.

## Treat synthetic data as a derived source

Synthetic data can rephrase existing text, generate textbook-style examples,
distill a stronger model by training on its outputs, or create verified
exercises. TinyStories showed that
a narrow synthetic story distribution could teach coherent English to models
below ten million parameters [@eldan2023tinystories]. The phi-1 experiments
reported strong code-generation results from a 1.3B model trained on a curated
mixture containing synthetic textbook and exercise data
[@gunasekar2023textbooks]. WRAP mixed real C4 text with model-generated
rephrasings and improved efficiency in its tested setting [@maini2024rephrasing].

These results do not make generated tokens automatically cheap, factual, novel,
or useful. Generation consumes inference compute; verification adds cost; and a
generator can reproduce benchmark content, source errors, or a narrow style.
Recursive replacement of original data by outputs from successive model
generations is the high-risk collapse setting studied by Shumailov et al.;
synthetic augmentation with preserved original data is a different regime
[@shumailov2024collapse].

Every generated record should retain its parent source IDs, generator provider
and checkpoint, prompt or template version, decoding settings, timestamp,
verifier result, and applicable usage terms. Evaluate factual fidelity,
diversity, source coverage, contamination, and downstream performance before
assigning a synthetic mixture weight.

## Decontamination protects an evaluation claim

Deduplication asks whether training records repeat one another. Decontamination
asks whether training data contains protected evaluation material. The second
question needs a frozen registry of benchmark versions before curation begins.

Whole-document Jaccard is a poor detector when a short benchmark item is copied
into a long page. For evaluation item $e$ and training document $d$, the
following formula defines an evaluation-side $n$-gram containment score:

$$
C_n(e,d)=\frac{|G_n(e)\cap G_n(d)|}{|G_n(e)|}.
$$

The symbols mean the following: $G_n(z)$ is the set of normalized token
$n$-grams in text $z$; $n$ is the chosen sequence length; $C_n(e,d)$ is the
fraction of the evaluation item's
$n$-grams found in the training document. A policy may flag a pair when
$C_n(e,d)\geq\tau$, where $\tau$ is a benchmark-specific threshold. The
normalization, $n$, common-gram suppression, retrieval method, threshold, and
adjudication rule all belong in the report.

Lexical matching misses leakage that changes the wording. Paraphrases,
translations, code rewrites, and synthetic restatements can preserve the answer
while sharing few surface strings. Yang et al. demonstrated such evasions and
found overlap in synthetic datasets [@yang2023rethinking]. Semantic or
model-assisted review can increase coverage, but it introduces its own errors. A
decontamination report proves what was checked and removed; it cannot prove that
no leakage exists.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Constraint arrow

Evaluation constrains data preparation. @sec-benchmarks must supply protected
item versions and registry digests before the final corpus build. The data and
evaluation teams jointly specify matching and adjudication rules. Confirmed
matches are removed or quarantined before training; after training, suspect
evaluation items can only be excluded and disclosed, not retroactively removed
from the model.
:::

The hand-off should contain benchmark and corpus version hashes, detector and
normalization versions, thresholds, reviewed samples, removal counts by source
and benchmark, removed token totals, and before-and-after corpus manifests. Use
opaque record IDs for restricted material rather than copying private data or
benchmark answers into a broadly visible report.

## Make every accepted record traceable

Live URLs change, so reproducibility rests on frozen inputs. Freeze raw
snapshots and accepted shards as immutable, content-addressed objects.
Rebuilding from those inputs with pinned code should reproduce the recorded
membership and shard checksums. Re-fetching a live source creates a new corpus
version.

A machine-readable manifest should contain at least:

```yaml
corpus:
  id: <stable corpus name>
  version: <semantic version>
  owner: <responsible team>
  intended_uses: [...]
  excluded_uses: [...]
source_record:
  uri_or_revision: <WARC record, URL, or repository commit>
  retrieved_at: <timestamp>
  raw_digest: <content hash>
  origin: <human, model-generated, or unknown>
  rights_evidence: <license, terms, consent, and dated evidence>
pipeline:
  code_commit: <revision>
  environment_digest: <container and dependency digest>
  transforms: <models, thresholds, seeds, and configurations>
  stage_counts: <accepted and rejected counts by reason>
lineage:
  parent_record_ids: [...]
  dedup_cluster_id: <stable cluster>
  retained_representative: <stable record ID>
evaluation:
  registry_digest: <protected benchmark versions>
  detector_policy: <normalization, matching, thresholds, review>
output:
  tokenizer_digest: <pinned tokenizer>
  shard_digests: [...]
  sampling_policy: <weights and schedule>
  consumed_by_runs: [...]
  tombstones: <removals and affected descendants>
```

The public datasheet can summarize purpose, sources, transforms, known
limitations, and slice statistics. Sensitive raw records, personal information,
and protected benchmark material remain access-controlled. Dolma illustrates
the value of publishing both corpus documentation and curation tooling
[@soldaini2024dolma]; Datasheets for Datasets provides a broader documentation
framework [@gebru2021datasheets].

## Validate the corpus before the full run

Before a corpus receives a full training budget, it should pass checks at
several scales:

1. **Stage accounting.** Reconcile document, byte, and token counts before and
   after every transform. Investigate unexpected retention jumps.
2. **Reviewed samples.** Sample accepted and rejected records by source,
   language, score band, and policy reason. Estimate errors with uncertainty.
3. **Distribution comparisons.** Measure which domains, languages, hosts,
   licenses, and document types each stage adds or removes.
4. **Duplicate audits.** Report exact, span, and fuzzy cluster distributions,
   including the largest clusters and representative policy.
5. **Contamination audits.** Run the frozen registry against every path into the
   corpus, including synthetic and imported datasets.
6. **Sampler tests.** Generate a dry-run stream and verify realized weights,
   effective epochs, ordering, packing, and shard balance.
7. **Compute-matched ablations.** Train small models with one data decision
   changed at a time, then compare held-out loss and target slices.
8. **Replay and removal.** Trace sampled records backward to sources and a
   source forward to all descendants and consuming runs.

Before committing the full run, record the acquisition snapshots, policy basis,
retained membership, filter audits, mixture weights, schedule, effective epochs,
decontamination limitations, tokenizer version, and output shard hashes. That
record makes the learned distribution inspectable and gives later evaluation a
defensible account of what the model could have seen. @sec-training-stack
carries this record into a working stack, as a data manifest that the training
job reads by digest, next to the open pipelines that produce the shards.
